Product-Led Growth: Letting the Product Sell Itself

Can the product sell itself, and what does that require of it? The story of a finance-software company in Bengaluru that had to answer the question with real numbers, not conviction.

1. A board meeting in Bengaluru

On the second Monday of January 2026, Priya Raman, VP of Product at Buland Systems, sat down to prepare a slide she did not want to present. Buland Systems built workflow-automation software that reconciled bank statements, vendor invoices and ERP ledgers for mid-sized Indian companies — the unglamorous plumbing that finance teams depend on and rarely think about until it breaks. The company had grown from zero to ₹42 crore in annual recurring revenue in five years, entirely through a sales-led motion: fourteen enterprise account executives, each carrying a quota built around an average contract value of ₹18 lakh a year, closing deals after a sales cycle that averaged nine months and involved a product demo, a security questionnaire, a pilot, and at least three rounds of procurement negotiation.

The problem was in the growth-rate column. Buland Systems had grown 61% year-on-year in 2023 and 44% in 2024. The board deck Priya had to present now showed 22% for 2025 — the deceleration was not a blip, it was a trend line, and three of the last five deals the sales team had lost were lost not to a superior competitor but to Belan Cloud, a two-year-old rival that let a finance analyst sign up with a work email, connect one bank account, and start reconciling transactions the same afternoon, for free, with no salesperson involved at any point until the analyst's own company had grown dependent on it. Buland Systems required a sales conversation to see so much as a live demo.

The board's instinct was to fix a sales-motion problem with more sales motion: double the account-executive headcount, at a fully loaded cost of roughly ₹6 crore a year, and hope volume closed the gap. Priya's instinct, watching Belan Cloud take deals in the ₹2–5 lakh segment that Buland Systems' sales team considered too small to chase, was different. She believed the company needed a second engine entirely — one where the product, not a person, did the work of getting a prospect to the point of paying. She had eleven days before the board reconvened to decide, and she needed to be able to explain — with arithmetic, not slogans — what that engine was, what it would cost, and where it would and would not work for a product like Buland Systems'.

2. The idea, precisely

Product-led growth (PLG) is a go-to-market motion in which the product itself does the primary work of acquiring, converting and expanding customers — by letting a prospective user experience real value before anyone asks them to pay, and by using what the product observes about their usage to decide when, and to whom, to present a monetisation moment or route in a human salesperson. It stands in contrast to a sales-led motion, where a person qualifies and persuades the prospect before they ever touch a working version of the product, and a marketing-led motion, where advertising and content do the persuading and a form-fill is the primary conversion event.

It is worth being exact about where this sits inside a bigger idea the reader may already have encountered: a go-to-market (GTM) strategy is a company's overall answer to the question of how it will reach, convince and retain the customers it wants — which channels, which motions, which segments, in what sequence. PLG is not a synonym for GTM strategy; it is one motion a GTM strategy can choose, alongside sales-led, marketing-led and partner-led motions, and mature companies frequently run more than one at once for different segments of the same product.

The term was popularised around 2016 by Blake Bartlett at OpenView Venture Partners, who was trying to name a pattern he saw across the portfolio: companies like Atlassian, Dropbox and Slack had built businesses of extraordinary scale with comparatively small sales organisations, because their products were simple enough, and valuable enough quickly enough, that individuals and small teams adopted them without anyone selling to them. The underlying practices — freemium pricing, self-serve signup, viral loops inside the product — existed earlier and had been documented piecemeal by growth practitioners such as Andrew Chen and SaaS-metrics writers such as David Skok; PLG was the name that tied the pattern together into a motion a company could deliberately choose and design for, rather than a lucky accident of a particular product category.

The single sentence Priya could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this one, and it is the sentence worth memorising because everything else in this page is an elaboration of it:

"Let the product prove its value to the user before you ask the company to pay for it."

3. How it actually works, step by step

PLG is not simply "remove the salesperson." It relocates the work a salesperson used to do — qualifying, persuading, timing the ask — into the product's design and its instrumentation. Walking through the mechanics with Buland Systems as the running example makes visible several steps that practitioners routinely leave implicit, because they are unglamorous compared to the idea of virality.

Step one — define and engineer the "time-to-value" moment. Before anything else, a team must decide precisely what the user must experience, and how fast, for the product to have proven itself without human help. For Buland Systems, Priya defined this as: a finance analyst connects one bank account or ERP export, and the product automatically reconciles at least ₹10 lakh of transactions with no manual matching. Everything in the self-serve product had to be redesigned to get a new signup to that moment in under an hour, not the multi-week implementation that enterprise deployments took.

Step two — build the self-serve path to that moment. This meant a signup flow requiring only a work email, no credit card, and no salesperson gate; a guided first-run experience; and a free tier generous enough to reach the aha moment but narrow enough (Buland Systems capped it at one workflow and 500 transactions a month) that real usage created real pressure to upgrade.

Step three — instrument usage, not just signups. The product had to emit events: account connected, workflow created, transactions reconciled, second user invited. This is the step most often skipped or done badly, and it is the one that turns a signup counter into an actual growth engine, because it lets the company distinguish a curious visitor from an account that is genuinely dependent on the product.

Step four — define the product-qualified lead (PQL) and product-qualified account (PQA). A PQL is an individual user whose in-product behaviour indicates real intent to buy — for Buland Systems, a user who connected a live account and ran a workflow at least five times in fourteen days. A PQA extends this to the account level: multiple users at the same company doing this independently, which signals organisational, not just individual, dependence. This distinction matters and is explored further in the topic this page unlocks, on product-led sales.

Step five — place monetisation gates at the moment of expanding value, not at the front door. Buland Systems' free tier hit its wall exactly where usage started to hurt — the 500-transaction cap — rather than gating basic access itself, which would have prevented anyone from ever reaching the aha moment in the first place.

Step six — design for expansion inside the account, and virality across accounts. A workflow that one analyst built could be shared with a colleague for approval, which is both a genuine product feature and a growth loop: it introduces a second user, at near-zero marginal cost, who might independently become a PQL.

Step seven — route qualified accounts to a human, on purpose and at the right moment, and treat this as a hybrid motion rather than a replacement for sales. This is the step Priya's board most needed to hear, because it is the one that resolves the anxiety that PLG means firing the sales team.

Figure 1. The product-led growth flywheel. Each stage is a design decision, not a hope — activation and monetisation are engineered, not left to chance.

4. A worked example, with the arithmetic shown

Set beside this was the cost side. A sales-led customer at Buland Systems cost roughly ₹5.4 lakh to acquire once the fully loaded cost of an account executive, sales-engineering support and a nine-month cycle were amortised across the deals that AE closed in a year. A self-serve paying customer, by contrast, cost approximately ₹42,000 — almost entirely the marketing spend required to generate the 20,000 monthly visitors, divided across the 63 who converted. That is roughly a thirteen-fold difference in acquisition cost per customer, which is the number that made the board lean forward, but it is not, on its own, the number that should have decided the question — because it says nothing about the size or durability of each customer relationship, a nuance the fourth section below returns to.

The more instructive exercise was a second pass, changing one input at a time to see where the leverage actually sat. If Buland Systems spent nothing extra on marketing but improved onboarding so that activation rose from 35% to 50% — a smaller technical lift than doubling ad spend — the funnel produced 1,000 × 0.50 = 500 activated accounts, and at the same 18% paid-conversion rate, 90 paying customers, or ₹1.62 crore in new ARR: a 43% increase in monthly output for zero additional acquisition spend. Conversely, if the company skipped Step Four above and let sales chase every signup indiscriminately rather than only PQLs, the resulting friction and mis-targeted outreach was modelled to drag the paid-conversion rate down to roughly 10%, producing only 35 paying customers and ₹63 lakh — a 44% fall from the base case, from a single organisational mistake rather than any change in the top of the funnel. The lesson Priya drew, and the one worth remembering independent of Buland Systems' specific numbers, is that in a PLG motion, activation and qualification discipline typically have more leverage on revenue than acquisition volume does, because they act as a multiplier on every visitor already arriving rather than requiring the company to find more of them.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

PLG is a motion; freemium is a pricing tactic

The two are routinely fused in casual conversation, but a company can run a self-serve, product-led motion with a 14-day free trial and a credit card required upfront and no permanent free tier at all — this is common in B2B infrastructure tooling where the audience is small and highly qualified already. Freemium is one way to get someone to the aha moment before payment; it is not the definition of PLG.

Self-serve is necessary but not sufficient

A signup form with no salesperson behind it is self-serve, but it is not yet product-led growth unless the product's own usage signals are doing the qualifying and expansion work that a salesperson used to do. Many companies believe they have "gone PLG" because they added a free trial, while sales still qualifies every lead manually from a form-fill, which is marketing-led with a self-serve veneer.

A signup is not an activation, and an activation is not a customer

The most common analytical error in this topic is treating the top of the funnel as the health metric. Table 1 above exists specifically to make visible that three separate rates — signup, activation, paid conversion — behave differently, respond to different levers, and must be tracked and improved separately rather than folded into one "conversion rate."

Where PLG applies, and where it structurally does not

PLG works best when time-to-value can be compressed to minutes or hours, the buying decision can be made by an individual or small team without a multi-stakeholder procurement process, and the product's value is legible without configuration. It works poorly for products that require deep custom integration before anyone can experience value, for genuinely regulated or safety-critical purchases where a compliance sign-off must precede any use, and for products whose real buyer (a CFO, a CISO) is organisationally distant from the person who would ever try a free trial.

What PLG cannot tell you

A well-run PLG motion accelerates whatever the product already is. It cannot fix a product that does not, in fact, deliver value quickly — it will simply reveal that fact faster and more cheaply than a sales-led motion would have, which is a genuine benefit, but a company must not mistake "our PLG funnel converts poorly" for a growth problem when it is actually a product problem. Nor can it tell a company whether it is leaving larger, more strategic accounts on the table by optimising for the segment PLG serves well.

The viral coefficient, precisely

Virality inside a PLG loop is not a vibe; it has an arithmetic definition worth knowing exactly. The viral coefficient, usually written k, equals the number of new-user invitations sent per existing user multiplied by the conversion rate of those invitations into new active users. If k exceeds 1, each cohort of users generates more than one new user on average, and growth becomes self-sustaining without additional acquisition spend; if k is comfortably below 1, as it is for most B2B products including Buland Systems' internal share-a-workflow feature, virality is a real but secondary contributor, and the acquisition and activation stages of the funnel still carry most of the weight.

PQL, PQA and MQL are different qualifications, and routing logic depends on knowing which is which

A marketing-qualified lead (MQL) is qualified by engagement with content — downloading a whitepaper, attending a webinar — and has typically never touched the live product. A product-qualified lead (PQL) is qualified by individual usage of the actual product. A product-qualified account (PQA) is qualified by usage patterns across multiple individuals inside the same company, which is a stronger signal of organisational, budget-holding intent than any one individual's activity. Sending a PQA-strength signal to sales as though it were a cold MQL wastes the single biggest advantage PLG creates.

The organisational question a newcomer should always ask

PLG is frequently mis-filed as a product team's initiative or a growth team's initiative, when it in fact requires product, marketing, sales, legal and support to move together — legal must pre-approve a click-through terms-of-service for self-serve signup instead of a negotiated contract, support must plan for a much larger number of low-touch accounts, and sales compensation must be redesigned so that account executives are rewarded, not penalised, for accounts that arrive via self-serve and later need a human touch to expand. Before trusting any PLG plan, a thoughtful newcomer should ask: who owns the activation-rate number, and does anyone's compensation plan actually reward protecting it?

Bindaas, a Mumbai-founded habit-tracking app, illustrates the consumer case: an individual downloads it, forms a habit streak within days, and invites friends largely for social reasons that have nothing to do with the company's revenue — the viral coefficient can genuinely exceed 1, and the monetisation gate sits behind a feature paywall rather than a usage cap. Buland Systems' case shows the more constrained B2B pattern: virality is real but modest, because the natural unit of adoption is a workflow shared with two or three colleagues, not a broadcast to hundreds of strangers, and the binding constraint is less about generating invitations and more about not undermining the existing enterprise sales relationship for larger accounts.

Bageecha, a fictional marketplace connecting small plant nurseries in Maharashtra and Karnataka to retail garden-supply buyers, illustrates a structurally harder version of the problem: PLG has to work on both sides of the transaction before anyone experiences value at all. A buyer with an empty marketplace to browse learns nothing about the product's value, and a nursery-seller with no buyers gains nothing from listing. Many marketplaces solve this by making one side genuinely self-serve and product-led — Bageecha let buyers browse and place trial orders with no salesperson — while accepting that the supply side needs concierge-style, human-assisted onboarding until there is enough buyer density to make self-serve listing attractive to a nursery on its own. This is a case where "just make it self-serve" as a blanket instruction actively damages the business, because it strands the side of the market with the least incentive to invest effort up front.

Company stage matters as much as product type. An early-stage company with no established sales motion uses PLG primarily as a cheap, fast way to discover whether the product creates real value and at what price — the self-serve funnel is a learning instrument as much as a revenue engine, and its numbers should be expected to be volatile and often disappointing at first. A large, established company layering PLG onto an existing enterprise sales motion, as Buland Systems was attempting, faces a different problem entirely: the risk is not whether PLG will work, but whether it will quietly cannibalise or demoralise the existing sales organisation, which is why the routing rule that sends any account above a defined size automatically to a human — rather than leaving it to compete informally with the free tier — is not an optional nicety but close to the central design decision of the whole exercise.

7. Common mistakes

Mistake one: treating PLG as "remove the salespeople." The symptom is a spike in support tickets and a rise in early churn shortly after launch, because signups that would previously have been filtered by a sales conversation are now filtered by nothing. The underlying misunderstanding is believing PLG eliminates qualification rather than relocating it into the product. The cheapest diagnostic: check whether a PQL definition exists and is tracked at all. If the only qualification event in the system is "filled in the signup form," the company has built a self-serve funnel, not yet a product-led growth motion.

Mistake two: chasing signup volume as the headline metric. The symptom is a marketing dashboard showing signups climbing steadily while paid conversion stays flat or falls. The underlying misunderstanding is conflating the top of the funnel, which marketing spend can move easily, with activation, which usually cannot be bought. The cheapest diagnostic is to plot signups and forty-eight-hour activations on the same chart across eight weeks; if the lines diverge, the marketing channel is buying low-intent traffic that the product was never going to convert.

Mistake three: a handoff to sales that is either too early or too late. The symptom, on one side, is account executives complaining that "PLG leads" waste their time; on the other side, it is an account quietly churning right after it hit a usage ceiling that should have triggered a human conversation. The underlying misunderstanding is not distinguishing a PQL from an MQL, or not instrumenting the threshold at which usage should trigger outreach at all. The cheapest diagnostic is to sample twenty accounts that upgraded and twenty that churned shortly after hitting a limit, and check whether a human touched either group at the right moment.

Mistake four: packaging and pricing left unchanged from the sales-led era. The symptom is either a free tier so generous that a normal team's needs are met forever, so nobody ever converts, or a paywall placed so early that nobody reaches the aha moment before being asked to pay. The underlying misunderstanding is designing the free tier as a marketing artefact rather than as the mechanism that carries a user from curiosity to dependence. The cheapest diagnostic is to overlay the free-tier limits directly on the map of what a user must do to reach the aha moment, and check whether the wall sits before or after that point.

8. What good looks like

Twelve months after that January board meeting, Buland Systems had a second engine running alongside its original one, not instead of it. The free tier was capped precisely at the point usage began to hurt — one workflow, five hundred transactions a month — rather than at the front door. A PQL was defined as a user who had connected a live account and run a workflow at least five times in a fortnight; a PQA existed once two or more people at the same company had done so independently. A small team of three product-led-sales specialists, distinct from the fourteen enterprise account executives, called only accounts that had crossed the transaction cap or shown a PQA signal, using the account's own usage history to open the conversation rather than a cold script. Self-serve had added roughly ₹9 crore of new ARR over the year at a blended customer-acquisition cost of about ₹38,000, against the enterprise motion's ₹5.1 lakh, and — critically for the board's original anxiety — enterprise deal volume for accounts above five hundred employees had not fallen, because the routing rule kept those accounts squarely with the sales team throughout. Blended company growth for the year came in at 47%, back above the 2023 peak, from two engines running in parallel rather than one engine run harder.

9. What Priya decided, and what to read next

Priya recommended, and the board approved, building the self-serve PLG motion as an additive "land" channel for the segment the enterprise sales team had been unable to serve economically — companies too small to justify a nine-month sales cycle — while explicitly protecting the existing enterprise motion for larger accounts through an automatic routing rule rather than an informal understanding. She rejected the alternative the board had originally proposed, doubling the account-executive headcount, not because it would have failed but because the arithmetic in Table 1 showed a channel with roughly thirteen times better acquisition economics sitting almost entirely unused, and because Belan Cloud's growth made clear that the smaller-company segment would be won or lost on time-to-value, a dimension no amount of additional sales headcount could improve.

The natural next topic to study from here is product-led sales — the discipline of building the PQL and PQA scoring, routing and hand-off mechanics that Buland Systems' new hybrid motion depended on, since a PLG funnel without a well-designed handoff to sales simply reproduces Mistake Three above at scale. Alongside it, a deliberate look at how a company chooses its overall go-to-market motion in the first place — of which PLG is only one option among several — clarifies the conditions under which this whole approach is the right tool rather than a fashionable one, and the virality mathematics touched on in Section 5 rewards a closer, more quantitative second look once the basic funnel is understood.

Two questions worth sitting with:

1. In your own organisation, who owns the activation-rate number — the percentage of signups who reach real value quickly — and would that person be comfortable admitting they do not track it weekly?

2. If your product's core value genuinely cannot be experienced within an hour of first contact, is product-led growth the right motion to reach for at all, or is the more honest next step to make the product faster to value before reaching for a growth motion it has not yet earned?

Buland Systems, Bindaas, Bageecha and Belan Cloud are illustrative composites used for teaching purposes and are not real companies.

Utthaan Stay Cloud: What Counts as a User?

A case on product-led growth, set in Shimla, in which the funnel's own definitions are the thing in dispute

1. The night before

On the evening of Sunday, 11 October 2026, the rain that had hung over Shimla since Friday broke, and Gunjan Katoch could hear water running off the tin roof of the Kali Bari Lane office. The board met at ten next morning, downstairs and on a bridge to Mumbai, Bengaluru and Toronto. The pack held one slide she had stared at for three hours.

It said that Utthaan Stay Cloud had added 38,400 property accounts in the year to 31 August 2026 and that 70 per cent had activated. It was the slide that had raised ₹28 crore in 2024, and everything on it was true. Katoch had stopped believing it in August, when a memo from Toronto argued that the word "activated", in Utthaan's own dashboards, had meant almost nothing since 2022.

Three decisions sat behind that word. The referral contract with Lahar Yatra Network, the trekking app that sent Utthaan more than half its sign-ups, renewed automatically on 31 March 2027 unless notice was served by 31 October. Hochtal Reisen GmbH of Munich wanted a white-label booking engine and had put ₹72 lakh a year against it. And her co-founder wanted ₹186 lakh to rebuild onboarding around a definition that would make every growth chart the company had published look wrong. The board had authorised ₹240 lakh, not all three.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2022

Katoch and Meghna Guleria founded Utthaan in 2020, when the hotels of Shimla, Kasauli, Manali and Dharamshala stood empty and their owners were learning that the agencies which had filled their rooms for a decade would not fill them again. The product was narrow and good: a "Book Now" page for an owner's website, Instagram bio or WhatsApp profile, with UPI and card collection behind it, and a channel manager that kept inventory in step across MakeMyTrip, Goibibo, Booking.com, Agoda and Airbnb, so a four-room property never sold the same room twice.

Pricing was product-led from the start. The Direct tier was free — a booking page, a payment link, a platform fee of 2 per cent on bookings collected through Utthaan. Pro, ₹9,600 a year per property, added the channel manager and rate rules; Suite, ₹24,000, added multi-property management and a revenue dashboard. No salesperson had ever called a customer, and the pitch decks said so.

The constraining decision came in spring 2022, when the seed money from Belwan Growth Partners was running out and the company needed a growth number. Fateh Rana's team in Bengaluru built the Instant Listing Importer: paste the URL of an existing listing and Utthaan pulled the photographs, room types and rates and published a live booking page in ninety seconds. Sign-ups tripled. Because a published page proved the importer had worked, the analytics team defined an activated property as one that had published a page. It was never revisited, and by 2026 it sat in the board pack, the investor updates, the Lahar contract and the growth team's objectives.

3. The industry

India's organised homestay segment grew quickly after 2021. Himachal Pradesh's home-stay registration rules, and comparable schemes in Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Goa, had pulled tens of thousands of family-run properties onto a formal register. UPI had solved collection: a guesthouse in Chail could take a ₹4,200 advance from a guest in Pune at no cost. OYO and Treebo had built branded supply at scale, while MakeMyTrip, Cleartrip and Booking.com remained demand engines a small property could not do without. Nobody in Shimla thought a guesthouse would go fully direct; they thought the direct share could go from a tenth to a third.

The software layer beneath that shift was contested. In June 2026 Belpatra Roomworks, a Dehradun firm that had raised ₹180 crore, launched a free-forever channel manager with no property limit and no transaction fee, monetising through a payment-gateway rebate. Utthaan's free tier suddenly looked expensive at 2 per cent. Overseas, operators like Hochtal Reisen sold Himalayan itineraries to Europeans and wanted infrastructure satisfying both the Digital Personal Data Protection Act and the GDPR — a burden nobody on the free tier had considered.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The reported funnel is Exhibit 1. Of 38,400 new accounts, 26,880 published a booking page, which the company called activation; 6,720 of those took a real booking within ninety days; 2,016 were paying at year end. The chain reads 70.00, then 25.00, then 30.00 per cent, and 2,016 of 38,400 accounts is 5.25 per cent.

Mihir Kanwar joined as senior data scientist in Toronto in January 2026 and spent two quarters rebuilding the event pipeline. In August he circulated a memo titled Four definitions of an activated property, now Exhibit 2, applying four tests to the same 38,400 accounts. On the company's definition, 70.00 per cent activated. Require also one manual rate or calendar edit — the owner touching the product rather than merely receiving its output — and 32.00 per cent qualified. A paid booking within ninety days: 17.50 per cent. Bookings in two months: 11.00 per cent.

His second finding was sharper. Paid conversion inside each population rose as the definition tightened: 7.50 per cent of the loosest, then 12.50, 20.00 and 25.00 per cent. The 26,880 activated properties were not a warm pool that had failed to convert. Some 14,592 never returned after the importer finished; their pages sat on the internet, unseen by their owners.

The third finding concerned where accounts came from. Lahar Yatra Network supplied 55.0 per cent of accounts and 26.2 per cent of payers; organic search, 16.7 per cent of accounts and 35.7 per cent of payers. The two cheapest channels — Sangh sponsorship and host-to-host referrals — supplied 21.7 per cent of accounts and 30.2 per cent of payers, and neither had a budget line.

Exhibit 5 complicated it again. In the cohort that first paid between September 2024 and February 2025, Lahar's properties retained 60.0 per cent of their logos and 68.6 per cent of their revenue two years on; organic properties retained 90.0 per cent of logos and 101.6 per cent of revenue. Whatever the contract bought, it was not what organic produced.

5. The people

Gunjan Katoch, co-founder and chief executive, Shimla. She has told the board for four years that Utthaan is product-led. Her incentive is a Series B in early 2027, for which the old growth chart is her strongest asset. She has not told Guleria that she asked Kanwar in July whether activation "held up".

Meghna Guleria, co-founder and chief product officer, Shimla. She wants the strict definition adopted now and onboarding rebuilt around it: a company that cannot say what a user is cannot iterate. She is not saying that the importer was her idea, or that a stricter funnel cuts reported sign-ups by two-thirds.

Fateh Rana, vice-president of engineering, Bengaluru. He can build the rebuilt onboarding or the Hochtal white-label, not both, and has said so in writing. He favours Hochtal: contracted revenue, and a problem his best people find interesting. He is not saying that two of them have offers elsewhere.

Zubin Parmar, head of supply and community, Solan. He built the Belaur Homestay Sangh relationship out of his own travel budget and runs the referral scheme on ₹4.32 lakh of credits a year. He believes Lahar rents Utthaan an audience it could own. He has not mentioned the Sangh's twice-offered advisory role, neither taken nor refused.

Mihir Kanwar, senior data scientist, Toronto. He wrote the memo and stands behind it. He is also the only one who says aloud that the multi-homing panel is self-selected and that his cohort covers 1,076 properties, not the base. He is thirteen and a half hours behind Shimla, and never in the room.

Firoza Jamwal, customer success lead, Singapore. She covers the sixty largest accounts, operators in Himachal, Uttarakhand and Goa, and has the clearest evidence that human contact converts: accounts she touched upgraded to Suite far more often. She wants four more people — but told Katoch she chose those accounts by size, so her uplift and their quality cannot be separated.

Geetika Sood, head of finance and revenue operations, Mandi. She points out, to Guleria's irritation, that Exhibit 4 shows a business, not a leak: ₹186.00 lakh of platform fees, 23.1 per cent of revenue, from properties that will never subscribe. Tightening activation may shrink the salaries.

Zehra Chauhan, board director, Belwan Growth Partners, Mumbai. She has told Katoch that the Series B market will not fund a company 55 per cent dependent on one referral contract. She has not said that Belwan's own mark values Utthaan on activated properties under the 2022 definition, and would fall if it changed.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

"I am not arguing that the number is a lie. I am arguing that it answers a question nobody asks. No owner in Kasauli wakes up wanting a booking page to exist. She wants a booking."

— M. Kanwar, memo to the leadership group, 19 August 2026

"Then say so on the slide. Put D1 and D3 side by side and let the board read both. What I will not do is change the definition four months before a Series B, then explain to twelve funds why activation fell from seventy to seventeen."

— G. Katoch, leadership call, 21 August 2026

"We explain it either way. Do it now and we found our own problem. Let diligence find it in March and we did not know."

— M. Guleria, same call

"Everyone looks at the top of the funnel. Fifty-five per cent of our sign-ups come from an app that is not ours, whose contract renews in March and whose roadmap we have not seen. My chapter leads cost less than the paid-ads budget and bring properties still here two years later."

— Z. Parmar, internal chat, 4 September 2026

"We would need data-processing terms signed before Christmas and a named contact in India. Our travellers' data cannot sit in a shared analytics table. Your free tier's terms are, forgive me, not written for Europe."

— M. Brenner, Hochtal Reisen GmbH, Munich, 23 September 2026

"Two of the proposals assume the growth we have continues. One assumes it does not. I would like the pack to say which the management team believes."

— Z. Chauhan, note on the draft board pack, 9 October 2026

8. The options as Katoch sees them

Option A — rebuild onboarding on the strict definition. Retire the importer as the default, require a verified payout account and calendar setup before a page publishes, rename the metric. Six engineers and two designers, ₹186 lakh, for ₹0.23 of ARR per rupee. Guleria's answer: the return is neither in year one nor in ARR, but in a funnel the company can iterate against.

Option B — renew with Lahar on their terms. A guaranteed 30,000 referred sign-ups, for keeping the ₹250-per-published-page fee, adding 18 per cent of first-year subscription revenue, and two years of exclusivity against rival itinerary apps. It is the cheapest line in Exhibit 6 and the only option that protects volume. It also pays Lahar on the definition Kanwar has just discredited: Utthaan would be buying published pages.

Option C — fund the channels that retain. Eight community managers across Himachal, Uttarakhand and Sikkim, doubled Sangh sponsorship, a wider referral reward: ₹112.32 lakh for 928 incremental subscriptions. The assumptions are the weakness. Nobody has tried to treble Sangh sign-ups, and the referral scheme's 9.00 per cent conversion comes from owners who already loved the product.

Option D — take the Hochtal contract. The best ratio on the page, and the only revenue contracted rather than forecast. It also takes Rana's best engineers off everything else for nine months, imports a GDPR obligation into a company whose free-tier terms were drafted in 2021, and makes Utthaan a vendor selling through a European operator rather than a product that sells itself.

Katoch had written the four on the whiteboard as a ranked list. What she had not written, and what Kanwar put in his memo's last line, was a fifth possibility: that the real product had never been the booking page but the channel manager, and that ₹186.00 lakh of platform fees was a payments business treated as a loss leader.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The board meets on Monday, 12 October. Notice on the Lahar contract must be served by 31 October or it renews to 31 March 2028 on existing terms. Hochtal wants heads of terms by 30 November and data-processing terms by end-December. The engineering freeze for the Kullu Dussehra and Diwali peak runs to 15 November, so nothing ships before then.

The money is tighter than the ceiling suggests. Cash is ₹474.30 lakh and burn ₹27.90 lakh a month: 17.0 months. The full ₹240 lakh adds ₹20.00 lakh a month, taking burn to ₹47.90 lakh and runway to 9.9 months before any new revenue lands. Options A, B and C together cost ₹332.65 lakh. Sood says anything above ₹150 lakh of net new spend needs the Hochtal cash or a bridge from Belwan, and Chauhan has not offered one.

Two constraints are not financial. The DPDP Act's consent and purpose-limitation duties apply to guest data flowing through 26,880 published pages, many owned by people who have never logged in; counsel in Chandigarh has asked, unanswered, who the data fiduciary is for a page its owner has never seen. And Belpatra Roomworks' free channel manager removes the option of waiting.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, state precisely what Utthaan's reported activation rate measures. Which definition would you adopt, and what does adopting it cost in that quarter?
  2. Lahar supplies 55.0 per cent of sign-ups and 26.2 per cent of payers. Does that make the contract good or bad, and what would you need to know that Exhibit 3 cannot tell you?
  3. Exhibits 3 and 5 rank the channels differently. Reconcile them. Which ranking should drive the 2027 budget, and what does that imply about how a product-led company should measure acquisition at all?
  4. Sood's platform-fee revenue comes from properties that pay no subscription. Are they a success of product-led growth, a failure of monetisation, or a different business — and what follows for Guleria?
  5. Jamwal's uplift and Parmar's referral conversion are real numbers from self-selected populations. Design a test, inside the ₹240 lakh ceiling and the 15 November freeze, that shows whether either scales.
  6. It is Monday morning, 12 October. What do you do, in what order, and what do you say to the board about the number on the slide that raised the last round?

11. Kali Bari Lane, late

At about eleven Katoch wiped the list off the whiteboard and wrote three phrases instead. Who is our user. Whose growth is this. What are we selling. Below them she wrote the two numbers she could not reconcile — 26,880 and 4,224 — and drew a box around neither.

Kanwar's last message, sent at 6.40 p.m. Toronto time and still unopened, read: "Whatever you decide, decide the definition first. Everything else is downstream of it, including the Lahar notice." Guleria had gone home saying she would support whatever went to the board, which Katoch did not believe.

The rain had stopped. Below the window the lights of the Sanjauli ridge were coming on, and somewhere among them, her map showed four hundred and eleven properties with a live Utthaan booking page whose owners had never opened the app.

Swayam Invoice Cloud: Can the Product Sell Itself?

A case on product-led growth for GST software aimed at small Indian traders

1. Opening

On Monday, 28 September 2026, Chetan Dahiya sat in the first-floor office of Swayam Invoice Cloud on Rohtak's Delhi Road, a printout of the sign-up dashboard in front of him. Outside, the Diwali buying season was gathering pace, and every consignment moving through the Rohtak mandi would need a tax invoice and, above a value threshold, an e-way bill. Sign-ups were climbing. Revenue was not climbing with them.

Dahiya, the company's founder and chief executive, had until the board meeting on Thursday, 15 October to propose how Swayam should grow over the next twelve months. The board had set a ceiling of ₹60 lakh of additional annual spend. He had three proposals and a suspicion: had the company been mistaking free sign-ups for demand, or could the product actually sell itself?

2. Company background

Swayam Invoice Cloud sells a self-serve web and mobile application that lets small traders issue GST invoices, generate e-way bills and file reconciliation-ready sales data without a chartered accountant in the loop. Dahiya, a former accounts executive at a Rohtak steel trader, founded it in 2021. The company raised a ₹6 crore seed round in 2023 and now employs 34 people.

The market is crowded and mostly benign. Tally remains the default desktop accounting tool for established businesses. Zoho Books and ClearTax serve firms with an accountant on retainer, and Vyapar has built a large base among the smallest shopkeepers. GSTN and the National Informatics Centre run the government portals into which every tool ultimately feeds, while UPI has made it easy to collect a subscription from a shopkeeper with a phone. Swayam's bet was narrower than any of these: a trader in a Haryana mandi town should be able to sign up, issue a first invoice and generate a first e-way bill in one sitting, in Hindi, without speaking to anyone.

Distribution had always been the product itself. There was no sales team. Customers found Swayam through search or a WhatsApp forward and signed up for a 30-day trial, then chose a plan and paid annually by UPI. Support was handled by a small team in Hisar led by Jitender Sheoran.

3. The situation

In the twelve months to September 2026, 1,20,000 people signed up. Exhibit 1 shows what happened next. Only 21,000 issued a real invoice within seven days and counted as activated, a rate of 17.5 per cent. Of those, 4,530 converted to a paid annual plan when the trial ended, which is 21.6 per cent of activated users and 3.8 per cent of all sign-ups.

Exhibit 2 breaks the same funnel by customer type, and here the aggregate hides a sharp split. Micro traders, typically one-person shops, were 72,000 of the sign-ups but activated at only 10 per cent. Small distributors with a godown, several staff and multiple GST registrations activated at 20 per cent. Goods-transport traders, for whom the e-way bill is a daily necessity, activated at 48 per cent. Once activated, the three groups also converted differently, at 10, 25 and 30 per cent, and paid very different annual fees. Micro traders contribute 17.28 lakh of annual recurring revenue against 99.00 lakh from distributors and 103.68 lakh from transport traders, so 40 per cent of sign-ups, the two stronger segments, produce over 92 per cent of revenue.

Three colleagues read these numbers from three vantage points. In Bengaluru, Vishal Lather, who leads a team of nine engineers, saw the 90 per cent of micro traders who never issued an invoice and blamed onboarding friction: too many screens, GSTIN look-ups that timed out on slow mobile connections. In Hisar, Jitender Sheoran saw distributors write in to support asking whether someone could set up their multi-GSTIN accounts for them. And with cash of ₹320 lakh in the bank against a monthly burn of ₹28 lakh, Dahiya knew the company had a little over eleven months of runway. Growth had to become more efficient before the next fundraise.

4. The people

Chetan Dahiya, founder and chief executive, Rohtak. He wants a plan the board will accept and that keeps the product's self-serve promise intact.

Pooja Kadian, head of product and growth, Rohtak. She owns the funnel. She believes the 90 per cent drop-off among micro traders is a product failure and that fixing it is the cheapest growth available.

Vishal Lather, engineering lead, Bengaluru. He supports Kadian and can deliver a rebuilt onboarding in two quarters, but warns that his team's Diwali-season release freeze runs to mid-November.

Jitender Sheoran, head of customer support, Hisar. Over six weeks he ran an experiment that the rest of the company is still digesting. He wants to formalise it.

Pradeep Nain, business development consultant, Sonipat. A former distributor, he believes Haryana's traders trust a person across a counter, not an app, and wants field sales built around chartered accountants and wholesalers.

5. Exhibits and the pilot

In July and August, two of his support agents phoned 300 distributor accounts that had crossed a simple threshold within their first 30 days: 100 or more invoices issued, or 20 or more e-way bills generated. The team called these accounts product-qualified leads, or PQLs. The agents offered to configure multi-GSTIN settings and explain the e-invoicing add-on. Of the 300 accounts, 120 converted, a rate of 40 per cent against the 25 per cent the segment achieves unaided. The 120 accounts chose a bundled plan at an average of ₹9,000 a year, against ₹6,000 for the standard distributor plan.

Across the full year, 3,000 of the 6,600 activated distributors would have met the PQL threshold. Exhibit 3 turns the three proposals into comparable numbers.

6. The options

Option A: rebuild self-serve onboarding. Hindi-first screens, automatic GSTIN fill, an e-way bill generated inside the first session. It is faithful to the product-led promise and helps every future sign-up, but its year-one return is the weakest, and the engineering freeze delays any effect.

Option B: sales assist on PQLs. A team of six, four in Hisar and two in Sonipat, contacts only accounts whose own usage shows intent. It keeps the product as the primary channel. The costs are a new function and a risk that the pilot's 40 per cent does not hold at 3,000 accounts.

Option C: field sales through chartered accountants and wholesalers. Twenty representatives would work the mandis of Haryana and beyond. Reach is real, but the cost is 180 lakh, 120 lakh above the ceiling, and it moves the company into a sales-led model.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, which segments does the product already sell to, and which does it not? What does the 48 per cent transport-trader activation tell you that the 17.5 per cent overall figure hides?
  2. What must a product satisfy before it can genuinely sell itself, and which of those conditions does Swayam meet for each segment?
  3. Is Sheoran's pilot evidence strong enough to justify Option B? What would you check before scaling it from 300 accounts to 3,000?
  4. Using Exhibit 3 and the runway, which option would you take to the board on 15 October, and what would you tell Kadian and Nain?

8. A note for the learner

Product-led growth asks whether users can reach value alone, and then where a human adds more than she costs. The disciplined answer sorts customers by whether they reach value unaided, measures what each segment pays, and adds people only where usage data shows purchase intent.

One defensible path is Option B. Its ratio of 1.17 rupees of new ARR per rupee spent is the only one above 1, and at ₹54 lakh it fits the ceiling with ₹6 lakh to spare. It rests on observed behaviour, and it preserves the self-serve engine: micro traders continue to sign up alone, and the team calls only the 3,000 accounts that have already shown intent.

The recommendation carries conditions. Gate the hiring in two steps: engage the first three agents, verify that the assisted rate stays near 40 per cent across at least 1,000 PQLs, and only then hire the remainder. Treat Option A as a second-half programme funded from the remaining ceiling, since the 90 per cent micro-trader drop-off is a real product problem that no sales team should paper over. Option C is premature: at ₹180 lakh it breaches the ceiling and would strain an eleven-month runway.

Product-Led Growth: The Fixed-Cost Bet

Product-led growth is usually taught as a cheaper way to acquire customers. It is more useful, and more accurate, to treat it as a decision to convert a variable cost into a fixed one — and to reason about everything that follows from that single substitution. Two companies, one month apart in the autumn of 2026, show why the difference matters.

This page assumes the reader already knows what product-led growth is: the self-serve funnel, the aha moment, the free tier, the product-qualified lead, the flywheel of acquire–activate–monetise–expand. It does not rehearse them. It argues instead for a particular reading of the mechanism, and spends most of its length on the places where that reading does real work: the arithmetic of fixed cost, the free tier with a non-zero marginal cost, the seams between organisations, and the questions on which competent people still disagree.

Section oneTwo decisions, thirty-one days apart

On the morning of 14 August 2026, Nandita Kulkarni, Chief Product Officer of Imarat Build Cloud, sat in a meeting room on the fourth floor of her company's office in Baner, Pune, with a consultant's slide on the screen behind her that she had not commissioned and did not agree with. The slide said, in forty-four-point type, Imarat must become product-led within eighteen months. The board had received it warmly. Nandita had thirty-one days, until the quarterly product council on 15 September, to turn the sentiment into a plan or to argue it down.

Imarat Build Cloud sold construction-execution software to mid-market residential developers: project scheduling, procurement against bills of quantities, site quality checklists, subcontractor billing, and the progress reporting that developers file to comply with state RERA authorities. It had reached ₹128 crore in annual recurring revenue across 340 customers — an average contract value of ₹37.6 lakh — through a sales motion of twenty-two account executives, each closing about four deals a year after an eleven-month cycle that touched, on the last count the revenue-operations team had done, a median of nine people inside the buyer. Implementation took fourteen weeks, because the product could do nothing useful until the developer's existing project master, vendor list and rate contracts had been migrated into it. Growth had fallen from 38% in 2024 to 29% in 2025 and was tracking 21% for 2026.

The board's enthusiasm had a specific cause. Ibtida Site Systems, founded in 2023 in Hyderabad, had put a free mobile application in the hands of site engineers — the junior civil engineers who walk a construction site each evening and record what was poured, what was delivered and what went wrong. The app did one thing: it turned that walk into a structured daily progress report with geotagged photographs, and it did it in under ten minutes, replacing a WhatsApp group and an Excel file. Ibtida claimed forty thousand downloads. Nobody at Imarat could establish how many of those were active, but two of Imarat's own customers had site engineers using it without anyone in procurement knowing.

Nandita's problem was not whether product-led growth worked. It was that the sentence "become product-led" did not describe a decision her company could take. Her platform's time-to-value was fourteen weeks and no amount of onboarding polish would compress a data migration into an afternoon. What she could plausibly do was carve out one narrow surface — the daily progress report — and let it be adopted without a salesperson. That raised a harder question than the board had asked: the field module in which the daily progress report currently lived appeared as a ₹4.8 lakh line item in 61% of Imarat's contracts, worth roughly ₹9.3 crore of the ₹128 crore. Giving it away free would be, by construction, a decision to destroy a known revenue line in exchange for an unknown distribution advantage. Vikram Sethi, her Chief Revenue Officer, had put it to her plainly over coffee: "You are proposing that I explain to twenty-two people that the thing they sold last quarter is now free."

Two weeks earlier and five hundred kilometres to the south-east, a different decision was coming to a head. On 2 September 2026, in a co-working floor in Gachibowli, Hyderabad, Aparna Iyer, co-founder and Head of Product of Ishara AI, was preparing for a conversation with her own CFO, Suresh Pillai, that she expected to lose. Ishara AI was nineteen months old. Its product ingested a company's historical support-ticket archive, learned the company's own resolutions, and produced an agent that drafted — and, once trusted, sent — replies to incoming tier-one tickets. It had reached ₹31 crore in ARR: 178 self-serve customers at an average of ₹3.9 lakh, and thirty-two enterprise accounts, sold by three people, at an average of ₹75 lakh.

The free tier was the company's origin story and, Suresh argued, its current liability. Forty-one thousand three hundred workspaces had been created; nine thousand one hundred were active in the previous thirty days. Each active free workspace made, on average, 415 billable model calls a month, at a blended inference cost of ₹0.97 a call. The arithmetic was ₹36.6 lakh a month, ₹1.10 crore a quarter, ₹4.4 crore annualised — 14.2% of ARR, sitting inside cost of revenue, pulling the reported gross margin from a defensible 71% to a 57% that Suresh could not take into Series B diligence without a story. His proposal was a fourteen-day trial with a credit card at signup, and the permanent free tier closed.

Aparna's objection was not sentimental. She believed the free tier was the only continuously running experiment the company had: nine thousand live workspaces, each one a natural test of whether the agent's drafts were good enough on a corpus nobody at Ishara had ever seen, generating the labelled accept-and-reject data that its evaluation harness ran on every night. Kill it, and the company would still have revenue, but it would lose the instrument that told it whether the product was getting better. She also suspected, without yet having the numbers, that the cost was not evenly spread — that a small number of workspaces were responsible for most of it, and that the choice Suresh had framed as free-or-paid was really a choice about the shape of the free tier rather than its existence.

Both decisions turn on the same underlying structure, and neither is well served by the standard account of product-led growth as a cheaper channel. The argument of this page is that PLG is best understood as a bet that a company can convert the variable, per-deal, human cost of qualifying and persuading a buyer into a fixed, engineered, up-front cost embedded in the product — and that almost every hard question in the discipline is a consequence of the unforgiving nature of fixed costs. Fixed costs are indifferent to how good your product is. They only care about volume.

Section twoThe idea, its history, and who disagrees about it

A precise working definition, which will be used for the rest of this page: product-led growth is a go-to-market motion in which the functions a salesperson performs — attracting, qualifying, demonstrating, persuading, timing the commercial ask and expanding the relationship — are relocated from recurring per-deal human labour into the product's design and instrumentation, and financed by giving away consumption of the product itself. Two clauses in that sentence do most of the work. Relocated, not eliminated: the labour does not vanish, it changes form and, critically, changes cost behaviour from variable to fixed. Financed by giving away consumption: the free tier or trial is not a marketing gesture, it is the purchase price the company pays for the information and the trust that a salesperson would otherwise have generated.

The intellectual history is older and less tidy than the label. Four strands converged.

The first is try-before-you-buy distribution, which predates the web: the shareware economy of the 1980s and early 1990s, in which utilities were copied freely on floppy disks and bulletin boards and a minority of users paid an honour-system registration fee. It established empirically that a software business could exist in which most users never paid, and that the paying minority could nonetheless cover the whole cost base — an idea that was obvious in retrospect and shocking at the time, because it requires marginal cost to be near zero.

The second is the viral loop, whose canonical origin is the line appended to the bottom of every message sent through Hotmail in 1996 at the suggestion of its investors: an invitation to get a free account, embedded in the product's own output. This established the idea that distribution could be a feature rather than a budget line, and it produced the arithmetic of the viral coefficient that the field still uses, and still misuses.

The third is bottom-up enterprise adoption, associated most strongly with Atlassian, which from the early 2000s sold developer tools with a published price list and no field sales organisation at all, on the observation that the people who would use the product were technical, could evaluate it themselves, and could expense a small purchase without procurement. This was the strand that first made the motion a threat to incumbents, because it routed around the buying committee rather than persuading it. India's own clearest exemplars sit here: Postman, whose API tooling was adopted by individual developers years before any company bought a licence, and Zoho and Freshworks, both of which built substantial low-touch small-business motions alongside more conventional sales.

The fourth is the metrics canon — the body of SaaS financial practice built up through the 2010s around customer acquisition cost, lifetime value, payback period and net revenue retention. This is what turned a set of tactics into something a board could underwrite, because it gave the motion a comparison basis against the sales-led alternative.

The term "product-led growth" was coined in 2016 at OpenView Venture Partners to name the pattern the four strands had produced. What is worth noticing is what happened afterwards. Between 2016 and 2021, when capital was cheap, PLG was justified on the grounds of reach and speed: a free tier put the product in front of an unbounded number of people. From 2022, when capital became expensive, the same practices were re-justified on the grounds of efficiency: shorter payback, lower cost per customer. The tactics did not change; the argument for them did. And from roughly 2024, generative products broke the assumption that had quietly underwritten the whole edifice since the shareware era — that the marginal cost of serving a non-paying user is approximately zero. Ishara AI's ₹4.4 crore is what that break looks like on an income statement.

There is no single orthodoxy. There are at least five positions held by serious practitioners, and they disagree in ways that matter for the two decisions above. The table sets out what each would and would not sign.

School Core proposition it would sign Proposition it would refuse to sign Evidence it rests on What would falsify it
Distribution PLG is a channel choice. Pick it when its cost per acquired rupee of gross profit beats the alternatives; the product is an input to that calculation, not its subject. "Adopting PLG should change what the product is." Cross-sectional payback-period comparisons across venture portfolios. Evidence that payback advantage disappears once product-engineering cost is fully loaded into the channel.
Product-design Time-to-value is the growth strategy. A product that cannot deliver a noticeable outcome in one unaided session cannot be product-led, and no funnel work will rescue it. "You can layer a PLG motion onto an existing enterprise product without rebuilding it." The consistent failure of enterprise incumbents' self-serve trials to convert. A well-documented case of a high-configuration enterprise product achieving a self-serve motion at scale without architectural change.
Bottom-up PLG is an organisational insurgency: it works by letting the end user adopt before the buying committee is consulted, and its natural enemy is procurement, not price. "PLG is primarily a pricing strategy." The developer-tools and collaboration categories, where adoption preceded purchase by years. Categories where individual adoption is possible but never propagates to a purchase — which is what "shadow IT that stays in the shadows" looks like.
Sceptic / cost-conservation Go-to-market cost is largely conserved. PLG moves it from sales headcount into engineering, lifecycle marketing, infrastructure and support. The real gains are speed and information, not cost. "PLG companies have structurally superior unit economics." Public-company sales-and-marketing ratios, which do not separate cleanly by motion once growth rate and category are controlled for. A matched comparison, same category and growth rate, showing a durable total-GTM-cost gap.
Information The free tier's primary output is not revenue but a continuously running, high-sample experiment on value, pricing and product quality. Its cost should be part-charged to research. "Free-tier spend should be judged on conversion rate alone." Companies whose roadmap and pricing decisions demonstrably improved after instrumenting a large free population. Evidence that the same learning is obtainable from a much smaller paid or panel population at lower cost.
Table 1. Five defensible positions on what product-led growth is for. The distribution and cost-conservation schools disagree about a measurable fact — whether total go-to-market cost is genuinely lower — and the evidence is not settled, mainly because public comparisons confound motion with category, growth rate and stage.

Notice that Suresh Pillai and Aparna Iyer are, without using the vocabulary, arguing from the sceptic school and the information school respectively. Suresh's position is that the free tier's cost is real, appears in cost of revenue, and is only justified by conversions; Aparna's is that a meaningful share of it is research spend misfiled as cost of goods sold. Neither is being obtuse. They are disagreeing about what the free tier is for, and no amount of funnel analysis resolves that by itself.

Section threeMechanics in depth: the arithmetic of a fixed-cost motion

The competent practitioner knows the funnel. The expert knows the cost structure underneath it, and reasons about the funnel as a way of moving a break-even point. Start with the substitution.

In a sales-led motion the cost of acquiring a customer is approximately linear in the number of customers: each additional account requires an additional increment of a person's year. Imarat Build Cloud's number can be built from the bottom up. Twenty-two account executives at a fully loaded ₹68 lakh each is ₹14.96 crore. Add sales engineering, demand generation, sales leadership and the revenue-operations function, at ₹9.4 crore, and total go-to-market cost is ₹24.4 crore against ninety new customers a year: ₹27.1 lakh per acquired customer. Against a first-year gross profit of ₹27.8 lakh per customer (an ACV of ₹37.6 lakh at Imarat's 74% gross margin), payback lands just under twelve months. That is a respectable sales-led business.

In a product-led motion the shape changes. Nandita's team costed the daily-progress-report product honestly, which is rarer than it sounds: fourteen people for nine months to build the self-serve path, the billing and entitlement system, the event pipeline and the abuse controls, at ₹3.9 crore; ₹60 lakh for payments, tax and legal work; ₹1.1 crore for lifecycle marketing, content and the in-product education layer; and ₹60 lakh for support tooling and a community. Call it ₹6.2 crore in the first year, rising to about ₹7.4 crore at steady state as the surface grows. Almost none of it varies with the number of customers. The only genuinely variable cost is serving free accounts — dominated, in this product, by storing roughly forty geotagged site photographs per site per day, at about ₹31 per free account per month.

The temptation at this point is the comparison that thrilled the board: at seven hundred self-serve customers in year one, total cost of ₹6.87 crore divided by seven hundred is ₹98,000 per customer against ₹27.1 lakh, a twenty-eight-fold improvement. This number is true and nearly useless, because the two motions buy customers of very different size. A self-serve customer at ₹2,400 per site per month across four sites pays ₹1.15 lakh a year, contributing ₹81,650 of gross profit at a 71% margin. First-year payback on ₹98,000 of cost is therefore fourteen and a half months — worse than the sales-led motion's twelve. The cheap channel, on the board's own preferred metric, loses in year one.

The correct comparison between two go-to-market motions is not cost per customer. It is the multi-year contribution margin returned per rupee of go-to-market spend. Cost per customer flatters whichever motion serves the smaller customer.

Run that properly. Over three years, with the sales-led cohort's observed 93% annual gross revenue retention, a sales-led customer returns ₹27.8 lakh × (1 + 0.93 + 0.865) = ₹77.7 lakh of gross profit against ₹27.1 lakh of spend — a ratio of 2.87×. The self-serve ratio depends on two things, and the surprise is which of the two dominates. The chart below plots the three-year return per rupee of go-to-market spend for the self-serve motion as a function of annual volume, for three different retention assumptions, against the sales-led motion's flat 2.87×.

Figure 1. Imarat Build Cloud's self-serve motion, modelled at ₹6.6 crore of fixed annual cost, ₹9,672 of free-account serving cost per acquired paying customer, a ₹1.15 lakh ACV and a 71% gross margin. The three curves differ only in the retention assumed for the self-serve cohort. The horizontal line is the sales-led motion's actual performance.

Two readings of this chart matter. The first is the obvious one: the self-serve motion does not beat the sales-led motion until it is acquiring somewhere between nine hundred and thirteen hundred customers a year, and Nandita's own bottom-up estimate of the addressable population — about eleven thousand Indian residential developers running three or more concurrent sites, of which a 6% annual capture would be aggressive — puts her at roughly 660. On this arithmetic, the daily-progress-report product is not a cheaper acquisition channel. It is a more expensive one.

The second reading is less obvious and more important. The three retention curves are close together. Moving gross revenue retention from 70% to 95% — a twenty-five-point swing, the difference between a leaky self-serve business and an excellent one — shifts the break-even volume only from about 1,250 to about 920, a 26% improvement. Halving the volume, by contrast, roughly halves the return. In a fixed-cost-dominated motion, volume dominates retention. This is genuinely counterintuitive, because the retention literature is loud and the fixed-cost literature is quiet, and because in a sales-led business, where cost is variable, the reverse is true. An expert asked to diagnose a struggling PLG motion looks first at whether the addressable population can ever be large enough to amortise the build, and only then at churn.

The four-rate decomposition and the cost of a point

Within a given volume, output is a product of rates, which means every rate has the same percentage elasticity: a 10% relative improvement in activation and a 10% relative improvement in paid conversion produce identical revenue. The competent practitioner knows this. The expert draws the opposite conclusion from it to the one people expect. Because the elasticities are equal, the rate to work on is not the lowest one — it is the one with the lowest cost per relative point of lift. Imarat's team estimated, from comparable work, that a 10% relative lift in signup rate would cost roughly ₹40 lakh of paid-media testing and landing-page work and would decay; a 10% relative lift in activation would cost about ₹25 lakh of engineering and would persist; and a 10% relative lift in paid conversion would cost perhaps ₹12 lakh of pricing and packaging experimentation but was bounded, because conversion cannot exceed the share of users for whom the product is genuinely worth ₹1.15 lakh. The correct sequencing falls out of those three numbers, not out of which rate looks worst on a dashboard.

The free tier when marginal cost is not zero

Ishara AI's situation requires a different instrument. When serving a free user costs real money, the free tier stops being a fixed cost and becomes a variable one, and the whole fixed-cost logic above inverts: the motion no longer improves with scale, it degrades. Aparna's first move was therefore not to argue with Suresh but to measure the distribution rather than the mean.

Figure 2. Ishara AI's free-tier inference cost is extremely concentrated. The mean of 415 calls per workspace, which drove Suresh Pillai's proposal, is an artefact of the tail; the median workspace costs less than a hundred rupees a month to serve.

The distribution changes the question entirely. A blanket closure of the free tier would remove ₹36.6 lakh of monthly cost and, with it, all nine thousand live experiments. A cap that binds only on the tail — four hundred agent-drafted replies a month, above the ninety-fourth percentile of usage — removes most of the cost while leaving the median workspace untouched. The general principle, which applies well beyond AI products, is that free-tier limits should be set from the cost distribution, not from a product manager's intuition about generosity, and that the limit that matters is almost always a ceiling on the tail rather than a floor on the median.

The steps everyone leaves implicit

Six pieces of work sit between a self-serve design and a self-serve business, and in the Indian market three of them are harder than they are elsewhere.

Payments and involuntary churn. Recurring card payments in India operate under the Reserve Bank of India's e-mandate framework, which requires additional-factor authentication when a mandate is registered, a pre-debit notification to the customer, and a further authentication step for debits above the prescribed limit. The practical consequence for a low-value self-serve subscription is that the silent monthly renewal that Western PLG playbooks assume simply does not happen reliably. Ilaaka Commerce Cloud, discussed below, found that 1.9 points of its 4.4% monthly logo churn were pure payment failure; it recovered 1.1 of them by offering UPI AutoPay alongside cards and rebuilding its dunning sequence. An Indian self-serve business that optimises onboarding before it optimises collection is working on the wrong end of the funnel.

Consent and data protection. A self-serve signup flow is the moment at which a company takes on data-fiduciary obligations under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and it does so without a negotiated contract to define the terms. Purpose limitation, itemised notice and a workable consent-withdrawal path have to be built into the product rather than written into a master services agreement. Teams routinely discover this in week eleven of a twelve-week build.

Tax and invoicing. Place-of-supply determination, GSTIN capture and validation at signup, and e-invoicing thresholds all have to be handled by software, for invoices small enough that a single manual intervention destroys their margin.

The remaining three — abuse and fraud controls on the free tier, a support model designed for volume rather than relationship, and the redesign of sales compensation so that an account executive is rewarded rather than penalised when a self-serve account lands in their territory — are universal, and the last of them is the one that most often decides whether the motion survives its second year.

Second-order effects

Five consequences follow from a PLG launch that are not visible in the funnel and that experienced practitioners plan for in advance. The free tier permanently resets the price ceiling for the capability it contains, in your market and not only in your company, because competitors must now match it. Self-serve support load grows super-linearly with account count until a deflection layer exists, because the accounts that arrive without a salesperson also arrive without an implementation consultant. Retention curves get worse before they get better, since the cohort now includes people a salesperson would have filtered out; a board that has not been warned will read the first four months as failure. The free population becomes a compliance surface: free workspaces inside regulated enterprises are shadow IT, and the first time a bank's information-security team discovers thirty of them, the company's response determines whether you become a vendor or a banned domain. And the free tier trains your competitors, who will evaluate you thoroughly, at your expense, and price against what they find.
