There are also four situations in which the idea is not merely inapplicable but actively misleading, and in which a competent team can do real damage by applying it faithfully.

The first is when a poor conversion rate is a value problem wearing a funnel problem's clothes. A PLG motion is an unusually honest instrument: it tells you, cheaply and at scale, that people who try your product do not want it. Teams that have committed to the motion are strongly inclined to read this as an onboarding defect, and will spend two years improving activation on a product nobody would pay for. The diagnostic that separates the two is to take the fifty accounts with the highest observed activation depth and ask what share of them converted; if even the deepest users do not pay, the problem is not the funnel.

The second is negative selection. A generous free tier does not sample the market randomly. It over-recruits the price-sensitive, the hobbyist, the student and the competitor's analyst — precisely the population least likely to pay and most likely to file detailed, articulate, well-argued feature requests. A roadmap built from free-tier feedback drifts steadily towards a product optimised for people who will never buy it. The tell is a feature request queue whose top ten items come overwhelmingly from accounts with no payment method on file.

The third is a small, concentrated market. If the entire addressable set is four hundred buyers, the fixed cost never amortises, and the free tier does something worse than fail to pay for itself: it surrenders the only leverage you have in the four hundred negotiations that constitute your business. Giving a capability away to a market of four hundred is not distribution, it is a unilateral price concession.

The fourth is when trying the product is itself the regulated act. In clinical, financial-advice and certain safety contexts, the question is not whether the user can get value quickly but whether they are permitted to use the product at all before a contract, a data-processing agreement and an audit exist. Inayat Care Systems, a Chennai company selling clinical documentation software to multi-speciality hospital chains, cannot let a physician upload real patient records into a free workspace, and no amount of onboarding design changes that. Its answer — discussed in the next section — is instructive precisely because it stops pretending to be a growth motion.

Section fiveHard edge cases and what the seams look like

Multi-product companies and the packaging trap

A single-product company has one free tier and one paywall. A three-product company has to decide whether the free tier belongs to a product or to the account, and either answer creates a problem. Ilaaka Commerce Cloud, a Gurugram firm selling storefront, order-management and warehouse software to direct-to-consumer brands, put the free tier on the storefront because that was the product with the fastest time-to-value. The consequence, discovered eighteen months later, was that its cross-sell into order management required a paywall that sat directly across the path a free storefront user had to walk to experience any value from the second product at all. The free tier had been designed to maximise adoption of product one and, in doing so, had made products two and three structurally harder to sell than they had been under the old sales motion. The general rule an expert applies is that in a multi-product company the free tier must be scoped to a workflow that terminates cleanly, not to a product, and the paywall must sit at the boundary of a new job rather than in the middle of an existing one.

Two-sided markets and the asymmetry of loops

Ishtihaar, a Mumbai platform matching regional-language content creators with consumer brands running campaigns, is a useful illustration of a failure that looks like a success. Its creator side is genuinely product-led: creators sign up free, build a media kit in twenty minutes, and recruit other creators at a measured viral coefficient of about 1.3, because a creator's status in the community rises with the size of the network they are part of. Its brand side is not product-led at all: a brand's coefficient is about 0.06, brand marketers do not refer competitors, and a brand experiences no value until enough matched creators exist for a campaign to fill. Ishtihaar spent its first two years optimising the side that was already working, because that side produced beautiful growth charts. The expert reading is that in a two-sided market the binding constraint is always the side with the lower coefficient and the higher value per participant, and effort spent on the other side is, past a threshold, pure waste. The correct sequencing is usually a hand-built, concierge, thoroughly unscalable motion on the constrained side, sustained for far longer than anyone is comfortable with, with PLG confined to the abundant side.

Regulated products: when the sandbox is the answer and the answer is not growth

Inayat Care Systems could not offer a free tier on real data. What it built instead was a synthetic-patient sandbox: a fully populated demonstration hospital, twenty-five minutes of guided path, and an output a consultant physician could evaluate on clinical merit without any of their own records entering the system. This works, and its numbers are honest about the cost. Activation in the sandbox runs at 22% against the 55–60% Ishara sees on real data, because a physician evaluating synthetic records is judging a demonstration rather than experiencing an outcome. Real time-to-value — the first moment a doctor's own dictation becomes a usable note — averages eleven days, gated by a one-page data-processing addendum that legal has pre-approved and that a hospital's medical superintendent can sign without procurement. Inayat's leadership stopped calling this product-led growth around the middle of 2025 and started calling it demand generation, which is both more accurate and more useful, because it moved the metric they reported from conversion rate to qualified pipeline and stopped them optimising a number that could not move.

Hardware plus software: the free tier is the second unit

Indriya Devices, of Coimbatore, sells connected industrial energy meters at ₹11,400 a unit to factories and commercial buildings, with an analytics application on top. There is no such thing as a free meter. What Indriya discovered, and then deliberately engineered, is that the software surface can generate hardware demand without a salesperson. Its analytics app contains a site-comparison view that is useless with one meter and valuable with three, because the insight a facilities manager actually wants is not "this line drew 412 kWh" but "this line draws 31% more than the equivalent line in the other shed." Of 4,100 single-meter accounts, 38% bought at least one additional meter within nine months, averaging 2.4 additional units: 3,739 meters, ₹4.26 crore of hardware revenue, generated by a software feature and an in-app purchase flow. The structural point generalises beyond hardware: the most reliable product-led expansion loop is a feature whose value is a function of the quantity of the thing the customer buys. Seats, sites, meters, connected sources, warehouses — the mechanism is identical, and the design question is always "what becomes possible at n+1 that is impossible at n."

AI-native products: activation becomes probabilistic

The deepest change generative products make to this discipline is not cost, although cost is what shows up first. It is that activation stops being deterministic. In a conventional product, if the user completes the steps, the value arrives. In Ishara's product, a user can do everything right and still see a mediocre agent, because the quality of the output depends on the quality and volume of the user's own archive — an input the company does not control and cannot see before signup.

Figure 3. For an AI-native product, activation is a function of an input the customer brings rather than a step the product controls. Thirty-nine per cent of Ishara's signups sat in buckets where the product could not work, and they consumed onboarding effort, inference budget and roadmap attention accordingly.

The conclusion Aparna drew from Figure 3 is the one that most offends conventional growth instinct: the right move was to make it harder to sign up. Requiring a connected archive of at least two hundred tickets before a workspace is provisioned cuts signups by roughly a third and raises blended activation from 36% to about 52% through selection alone, before any onboarding improvement at all. This is a legitimate move and an uncomfortable one, and it has a false-negative cost that Aparna insisted on quantifying: two of the twelve largest self-serve accounts acquired in the previous year would have been blocked by the gate, because they connected a small archive first and a large one later. The gate was therefore built as a soft one — a workspace below the threshold can be provisioned, but on a restricted path, with the frontier model withheld.

What happens at the organisational seams, and what mature companies actually do

Everything above is tractable. The seams are not. Four of them recur.

Compensation. The published version is a clean routing rule: accounts above a stated size go to sales, below it to self-serve, arbitrated by the system. The actual version, at almost every company that has run a hybrid motion for more than two years, is a quarterly meeting in which sales leadership argues that specific self-serve accounts were "really" sourced by the field, the rule is amended, and the amendment is reversed the following year. Experts do not regard this as a failure of governance; they regard it as the price of running two motions and budget time for it. What they refuse to accept is an ambiguous rule, because ambiguity is resolved in favour of whoever is most senior in the room.

Support. A sales-led business staffs support against relationships; a product-led one must staff it against events, with a deflection layer — in-product diagnostics, a searchable community, a status surface — built before the volume arrives rather than after. Companies that discover this after launch spend the following two quarters hiring support agents, which is the most expensive way to absorb a load that should have been designed out.

Security and procurement. The free population inside large customers is shadow IT. The mature response is to instrument it deliberately: know which free workspaces sit on which corporate email domains, build a self-service administrator claim flow so that a company's IT function can take ownership rather than demand deletion, and treat the first security enquiry from a large enterprise as the top of a sales funnel rather than an incident.

Finance. Usage-based self-serve pricing produces revenue recognition, forecasting and collection problems that a subscription business does not have, and it produces them at a volume of invoices that no controller can manage manually. The forecast, in particular, behaves differently: a sales-led pipeline is forecast from a small number of large, human-assessed deals; a self-serve book is forecast statistically from cohort behaviour, which is more accurate in aggregate and useless for answering "will we close the Ambuja account this quarter."

The last thing worth saying about the seams is the most deflating. The most common actual outcome of a large incumbent's "PLG transformation" is a self-serve trial serving the small-business segment, with the enterprise motion essentially unchanged, described internally as an incomplete transformation. In most cases that outcome is correct and the label is wrong. The transformation was never the point; reaching a segment the sales motion could not serve economically was.

Section sixThe nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Time-to-value is a distribution, and the median is the least informative statistic in it. A team that reports "our time-to-value is eleven minutes" has almost certainly computed a median over users who reached value, which conditions on the outcome and discards the people who never got there. The expert asks for the ninetieth percentile and, more importantly, for the shape. A bimodal distribution — a cluster at eight minutes and another at three days — is not one product with variance; it is two products sharing a signup form, and the right response is usually to route them differently at the door rather than to average their onboarding.

A free-tier limit sets a market price ceiling you cannot subsequently raise. Teams routinely say "we can always tighten it later," and the sentence is technically true and practically false. Tightening is paid for in trust, is asymmetric in its effects, and is remembered by exactly the users who talk publicly. The design discipline that follows is precise: choose a limit you expect to loosen, and be conservative at launch. The tell-tale sign that a team has not internalised this is a launch conversation in which the free-tier limit is described as a marketing decision, revised upward twice in the week before launch by people who will not own its consequences.

Conversion rate is a ratio whose denominator is a policy choice. Every gate a company adds to signup — a credit card, a work-email requirement, a minimum data volume, a qualification survey — raises the conversion rate and lowers the denominator. The number goes up; the business may have got smaller. The expert's reflex on hearing "conversion improved from 2.8% to 6.1%" is to ask for the absolute count of new paying customers, and, if it also rose, for the reason, because a rise in both is the only combination that means anything.

Activation must be defined as an outcome in the user's world, not a state in your database. "Completed onboarding" and "created a project" are not activation; they are compliance with your interface. Activation is the first moment at which the user would be annoyed if the product were taken away. The test that distinguishes the two is whether the event predicts retention: if a company's activation definition has no measurably different thirty-day retention from its non-activated cohort, the definition is decorative. Imarat's proposed definition — a site engineer filing daily progress reports for the same site on three consecutive working days — passed that test; the first draft, "uploaded a photograph," did not.

Virality in business software is collaboration, not referral, and it is bounded by the size of a team. Consumer viral loops broadcast to a network of hundreds. Business loops invite a colleague because the work requires it, which means the ceiling on a workspace's user count is the size of the team doing the job — six, or eleven, or four. A B2B growth model that projects a viral coefficient above one is almost always double-counting expansion within an account as acquisition of new accounts. The useful metric is not k but account penetration depth: the share of the relevant team inside a customer that uses the product, tracked as a distribution, because penetration is the strongest available predictor of both expansion and survival at renewal.

Retention curves get worse when a PLG motion launches, and this is the expected result of a correct decision. The new cohort includes people a salesperson would have filtered out, and they leave. What matters is not the first month's churn but whether the retention curve flattens — whether there is an asymptote, and at what level. An expert presents the board with a cohort chart at launch, before the numbers arrive, with the expected shape drawn on it, precisely so that the predictable deterioration cannot later be read as evidence that the motion failed.

Self-serve revenue and sales-led revenue are different financial assets and should not be blended into one retention number. Self-serve cohorts typically show lower gross retention and, in some categories, higher net expansion; enterprise cohorts show the reverse. A single company-wide net revenue retention figure that mixes them conceals both, and will mislead in a specific direction: growth in the self-serve book will mechanically depress the blended number even while it is creating value. The tell is a board pack with one NRR line. The expert asks for two, plus the mix shift between them, because the mix shift explains most of the movement.

The free tier's largest cost is usually not infrastructure but roadmap capture. Free users are numerous, engaged, articulate and unrepresentative. Their requests arrive in volume and their arguments are often better than paying customers', who are busy. Over eighteen months this quietly reorients a product towards a population with no willingness to pay. The countermeasure is procedural rather than analytical: every feature-request summary that reaches a prioritisation meeting must be segmented by payment status and by product-qualified status before anyone reads it, because segmenting it afterwards never happens.

Product-led and sales-assisted are not two points on a continuum; they are two qualification systems that must be reconciled inside one customer record. The practical form of this is dull and decisive: what happens when a marketing-qualified lead from a webinar and a product-qualified account from the free tier are the same company, with different owners, different scores and different next actions? A company without an explicit precedence rule and a deduplication key will discover it has two motions competing for the same account, and the account will notice. When an expert is shown a PLG plan, one of the first artefacts they ask for is the deduplication rule, and the absence of one is diagnostic.

The single most useful board metric for a PLG motion is the distribution of time from signup to first rupee. It is simultaneously a product metric and a finance metric, it cannot be gamed by moving spend between lines, and its tail tells you about the segment you are failing to serve. A company that knows its median self-serve customer pays on day nineteen and that its ninetieth percentile pays on day 140 knows something actionable about both its onboarding and its packaging. A company that knows only its conversion rate knows neither.

In India, instrument collection before you instrument onboarding. The e-mandate framework makes involuntary churn a first-order term rather than a rounding error in low-value self-serve subscriptions, and it is invisible in most analytics stacks because a failed renewal looks like a cancellation. The expert's diagnostic is a single query: of the accounts that lapsed last month, what fraction had a payment attempt that failed, and of those, what fraction was ever contacted? A business losing two points of monthly churn to card failures is losing roughly a fifth of its customer base a year to a problem that dunning, UPI AutoPay and a retry schedule largely solve, and no amount of onboarding work recovers it.

Two: Imarat Build Cloud finds that its PLG case is not an economic one

What changed the answer was a second calculation that had nothing to do with acquisition cost. Imarat's revenue-operations team went back through the twenty-three enterprise deals lost in the previous six quarters and found that in nine of them, a competing field application was already in use by the customer's site engineers at the time of the evaluation, and that in seven of those nine the customer's project managers had cited familiarity with the competitor's reporting format as a reason for preference. The average value of a lost deal was ₹34 lakh. If the free application recovered even three such deals a year, that is ₹1.02 crore of ARR and a durable defensive position, and the calculation is no longer a channel comparison at all — it is an estimate of the cost of ceding the site engineer to somebody else.

The commercial design that followed was tight. The free application covers up to three concurrent sites, permanently, with no user limit, because the loop is the second and third site rather than the second and third user. It does not include commercial reporting — subcontractor billing, cost-to-complete, variance against budget — and Nandita committed in writing that it never would, because that module is the boundary between a site tool and the platform, and the boundary had to be legible to the sales team as well as to the customer. The paid self-serve tier begins at the fourth site. The product-qualified account definition is two or more sites active for three consecutive weeks with more than one project manager reviewing reports; those accounts route to a three-person product-led sales pod, not to the enterprise team. And any account whose registered developer has more than fifteen concurrent sites — the enterprise threshold — is routed to the field team automatically at the moment of signup, before the free experience begins.

Three: Ilaaka Commerce Cloud, a failure and a five-quarter recovery

Ilaaka's story is the one worth studying, because it was executed competently and failed anyway. In the second quarter of 2024 it launched an unlimited free tier on its storefront product. Signups reached 9,400 a month by the fourth quarter. Conversion settled at 1.1%. Support tickets went from 3,100 a month to 19,700, and support headcount from 22 to 61. Fourteen of nineteen account executives were reassigned to work "inbound product-qualified leads" which, because no event instrumentation existed, meant every signup. Enterprise new-logo bookings fell from ₹6.2 crore a quarter to ₹3.7 crore. Net revenue retention fell from 111% to 96%, because the free tier served the same use case as the ₹7 lakh plan and existing customers downgraded into it at renewal. The Chief Product Officer left in January 2025.

The diagnosis, when it was finally done properly in early 2025, identified three errors that compounded. The free tier had been gated on volume — orders per month — rather than on capability, which meant that a small brand with genuinely simple needs was fully served forever, while the capabilities that actually distinguished the paid product (multi-warehouse inventory, multi-state GST e-invoicing, and API access) were available free. Qualification had been declared rather than instrumented, so "product-qualified lead" meant "signed up," and the sales organisation correctly concluded that the whole programme was wasting their time. And compensation had been left unchanged, so an account executive whose territory contained a self-serve customer received nothing for expanding it, while the same account, sold cold, would have paid commission.

The recovery took five quarters and three simultaneous changes. The gate moved to a capability boundary. Event instrumentation was rebuilt, which took seven months and delivered nothing visible in the interim — the single hardest thing to fund in a company that is already losing revenue. Compensation was rebuilt with an origination accelerator: an account executive who expanded a self-serve account received a higher rate than on a cold deal, on the argument that the company should pay for the outcome it wanted rather than for the effort it could observe. The account-executive team shrank from nineteen to twelve, all carrying enterprise-only quota. By the second quarter of 2026 the company was at ₹101 crore with ₹19 crore of it self-serve, conversion at 4.3%, and support headcount below its pre-launch peak on nearly three times the account count.

The honest summary is not that Ilaaka eventually succeeded. It is that a correct strategic decision, executed without instrumentation, without a capability-based gate and without a compensation redesign, cost the company roughly five quarters of growth and its Chief Product Officer — and that none of the three missing pieces was glamorous, expensive or intellectually difficult. They were simply not the part of the plan anyone was excited about.

Section nineFailure modes, their early signs, and the cost of late diagnosis

Negative selection and roadmap capture. Early sign: satisfaction scores from free users rising while paying-customer net revenue retention falls. Diagnostic question: of the top ten items on the roadmap, how many were requested by accounts with a payment method on file, and how many by product-qualified accounts? Cost of catching it late: two or three release cycles spent building for a population that will not pay, and a paid base that quietly begins to evaluate alternatives.

Free-tier cost drift. Early sign: cost per active free account rising month over month while conversion is flat. Diagnostic question: what does the ninety-fifth-percentile free account cost to serve, and what share of total free-tier cost sits above the ninetieth percentile? Cost of catching it late: for an AI-native business, gross margin becomes a financing blocker, and the remedy under time pressure is usually a blunt closure that destroys the informational value along with the cost.

The un-tightenable limit. Early sign: a free-tier limit that has not changed since launch and for which no single person can be named as owner. Diagnostic question: who is accountable for the free-tier P&L line, and when did they last change a limit? Cost of catching it late: by the time the limit must move, a public constituency exists to defend it, and the change costs more in trust than it recovers in revenue.

Channel conflict expressed as data behaviour. Early sign: a rise in accounts manually reclassified from self-serve to enterprise, or a fall in the completeness of CRM logging by the field team. Diagnostic question: what proportion of accounts crossed the routing boundary by a human override rather than by the rule, and did the overrides cluster around quarter end? Cost of catching it late: the routing data becomes unusable, which means the motion can no longer be measured, which means it can no longer be defended in a budget cycle.

Instrumentation rot. Early sign: an activation rate that moves by more than five points in a month with no corresponding product change. Diagnostic question: when was the event schema last validated end to end against a manual replay of ten real sessions? Cost of catching it late: every decision taken in the interim was taken on wrong numbers, and there is no way to know which ones.

Involuntary churn. Early sign: lapses clustering on renewal dates rather than distributed across the month. Diagnostic question: of accounts that lapsed last month, what fraction had a failed payment attempt, and what fraction of those was contacted within seventy-two hours? Cost of catching it late: a permanent two-point drag on monthly retention, compounding to roughly a fifth of the base each year.

Shadow-IT escalation. Early sign: inbound enquiries from corporate information-security teams asking for a list of users on their domain. Diagnostic question: can the company produce, within an hour, a domain-level inventory of free workspaces and an administrator-claim path? Cost of catching it late: a domain block at a large enterprise, which removes not only the free footprint but the sales opportunity, and which competitors will cite.

Solving a distribution problem with a pricing lever. Early sign: the free tier has been loosened twice in twelve months, each time in response to flat signup growth. Diagnostic question: what evidence exists that the constraint is willingness to try rather than awareness or fit? Cost of catching it late: the price ceiling has been permanently lowered, the underlying distribution problem is unchanged, and the company now has less room to respond.

Section tenWhere experts genuinely disagree

Does PLG lower the total cost of going to market, or only relocate it? The distribution school points to payback periods: cohorts of self-serve customers that recover their acquisition cost in months rather than quarters, and companies that reach substantial revenue with sales-and-marketing ratios far below their sales-led peers. The cost-conservation school responds that these comparisons load engineering, infrastructure, lifecycle marketing and support into research and development or cost of revenue, where they are invisible to the ratio being compared, and that a fully loaded accounting shows the gap narrowing to something close to nothing once category and growth rate are controlled for. This is a disagreement about a fact, and it is unresolved because the natural experiment does not exist: no company runs both motions on the same product in the same market with a clean allocation of shared cost. What would settle it is a matched study with product-engineering cost attributed by function rather than by department — which every company could do internally and almost none does, because the answer is uncomfortable for whoever is sponsoring the motion.

Permanent free tier or time-boxed trial? The freemium case is that a permanent free tier builds a population, a brand and a corpus of usage data that a trial cannot, and that the users who never pay are frequently the ones who recommend you to those who do. The trial case is that a permanent free tier selects against payment — it recruits and retains exactly the people for whom the free product suffices, gives them no forcing function, and leaves the company optimising a population it has trained not to buy. The evidence is genuinely mixed, and the honest reading is that the answer is category-dependent: in categories with strong individual identity and public artefacts, free tiers appear to pay; in categories where the product is invisible outside the buying organisation, trials appear to convert better. What would falsify the freemium case in a given company is a well-run holdout: cohort the free tier into permanent and ninety-day-expiring arms and compare two-year revenue, not ninety-day conversion. Very few companies have the nerve.

Can PLG be retrofitted, or must it be a separate product with a separate profit and loss? The retrofit camp argues that the alternative is to concede the low end and that a single product with tiered packaging is the only way to make the upgrade path real. The separation camp argues that a product built for a fourteen-week implementation has an architecture, a data model, a support culture and a compensation system that will reject a self-serve organ, and that the only reliable approach is to stand up a distinct product with its own team, its own price list and its own P&L, accepting that the migration path between them will be poor. Nandita's decision sits with the separation camp in substance if not in name. What would have to be true for the retrofit camp to be right in her case is that the platform's data model could accept a site created without a migrated project master — and it could not, which is why her answer was a separate application rather than a free tier on the existing one.

Is the viral coefficient a useful concept in business software at all? One position holds that it is: invitations are countable, conversion from invitation is measurable, and the arithmetic disciplines a team that would otherwise talk vaguely about word of mouth. The other holds that in B2B it is nearly always measuring expansion within an account and mislabelling it as acquisition, that its ceiling is the size of a working team, and that reporting it encourages exactly the wrong investment. The second position is closer to correct in most business categories, but it overreaches when it denies that cross-organisational loops exist — shared artefacts that reach a customer's customers, or a consultant who carries a tool between clients, are genuine acquisition loops and should be measured as such, separately from in-account invitations.

For AI products, should the free tier run on the best model or the cheapest? The best-model camp argues that the free experience is the product's only chance to form an impression, that a degraded free tier misrepresents what the customer would buy, and that the resulting suppression of activation costs more than the inference does. The cheap-model camp argues that the frontier model's cost is unbounded on a free population, that customers cannot reliably distinguish model tiers on routine work, and that the margin protection is worth several points of activation. Ishara's hybrid — a frontier-model showcase at first contact, a distilled model thereafter — is a compromise nobody argued for in the abstract, and it is not obviously right: Aparna's own concern was that a user who sees excellent output in week one and adequate output in week three learns something about the company that is worse than never having seen the excellent output at all. The experiment that would settle it is a model-tier split test measured on ninety-day retention rather than on activation, and it has not been run.

Is the "information value" of a free tier real, or a rationalisation? This is the disagreement in Aparna's own building. The steelman for the information school is that a large free population produces a distribution of use cases, failure modes and willingness-to-pay signals that cannot be purchased and cannot be simulated, and that in a fast-moving category this is the difference between a product that improves and one that ossifies. The steelman against is that most of the learning saturates quickly, that a panel of two hundred instrumented users and twenty deep interviews recovers the great majority of it at a fraction of the cost, and that "we learn from it" is the argument reached for when conversion cannot be defended. Both are right about different companies. The test Aparna eventually accepted was a falsifiable one: name, in advance, three decisions in the next two quarters that will be made differently because of free-tier data, and review at quarter end whether they were.

Section elevenWhat mastery looks like

Someone who has studied product-led growth can describe the flywheel, define a product-qualified lead, and name the metrics. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in six observable ways.

They start from the cost structure rather than from the funnel. Asked whether a company should go product-led, their first question is not about time-to-value but about the size of the addressable population and the honest fixed cost of the build, because those two numbers determine whether any funnel work can matter. They ask for distributions rather than averages, as a reflex, and they are visibly uncomfortable when handed a mean. They can name, for any free tier they are responsible for, the limit they expect to loosen next and the limit that will never move, and they can explain the difference. They treat the free tier as a profit-and-loss line with a named owner and a ceiling, rather than as a product decision with a cost side-effect. They design the routing rule and the compensation change before the onboarding flow, because they know which of the two has ended more PLG programmes. And they are willing to reduce the top of the funnel — to add a gate, to block a segment, to make signup harder — when the evidence says the removed population cannot get value, which requires a tolerance for a falling headline number that most organisations do not reward.

The clearest single marker, though, is negative. An expert is able to say "this product should not be product-led" and to say it to a board that has already decided otherwise, with the arithmetic that makes the statement checkable rather than merely contrarian. The competent practitioner, handed the same board slide, builds the best PLG motion the product can support, executes it well, and discovers in year three that the fixed cost never amortised.

Section twelveWhat each protagonist decided

On 15 September 2026, Nandita Kulkarni told the product council that Imarat Build Cloud would not become a product-led company, and that it would ship a free product-led application within two quarters. The apparent contradiction was the point of her presentation. The self-serve motion could not be justified as an acquisition channel: the break-even volume of roughly a thousand customers a year exceeded any credible capture of the market. It could be justified as a defensive move worth an estimated ₹1.02 crore of recovered annual ARR from enterprise deals not lost, plus an instrument that would tell Imarat, for the first time, what site engineers actually did each evening. She accepted the loss of the ₹4.8 lakh field-module line on new contracts, arguing that a line item competitors were giving away free had already stopped being revenue and had merely not yet stopped being invoiced. Vikram Sethi supported the plan on one condition, which Nandita granted: the fifteen-site enterprise routing threshold would be encoded in the signup flow before launch, not added afterwards.

Three weeks earlier, on 24 September, Ishara AI's executive team approved Aparna Iyer's restructure over Suresh Pillai's closure proposal, with Suresh's ceiling condition attached. The free tier survived with a hard cap, a soft signup gate and a two-tier model policy, and with a ₹65 lakh quarterly budget that Aparna owns and that tightens the cap automatically when breached. Suresh's stated reason for accepting was not that he had been persuaded of the information argument; it was that the restructure delivered the margin he needed without requiring him to win the argument. Aparna noted in the memo that she might be wrong in a specific way: if the distilled model's output quality degrades the free experience enough that ninety-day retention of converted accounts falls, the compromise will have bought margin with customer quality, and she committed to reporting that number at the end of the first quarter of 2027 whether or not anyone asked for it.

Discussion questions

1. Nandita justified a product-led investment on defensive grounds after concluding it failed on channel-economics grounds. Is that a legitimate use of the evidence, or is it the same reasoning she criticised in the board's consultant, arriving at a different conclusion? What would have to be true about the nine lost deals for her argument to hold?

2. Ishara AI improved every metric that mattered by removing a third of its signups. Under what conditions would that move destroy a company instead — and how would a team distinguish those conditions from Ishara's before acting rather than after?

3. Ilaaka Commerce Cloud's recovery required three changes made simultaneously: the gate, the instrumentation and the compensation plan. If a company can only fund one of the three this year, which should it be, and what does the answer reveal about which of the five schools in Table 1 you actually belong to?
